body:
![](/src/uploads/knee-ai-cover.png)

*Figure 1. AI-generated editorial illustration for terminalbio. The anatomy and image stacks are schematic, not patient scans or visualizations of our model’s reasoning.*

A knee MRI examination contains much more information than a single image. Different sequences and viewing planes reveal different aspects of ligaments, menisci, cartilage, bone, and fluid. A useful AI system must turn that collection into a structured assessment while preserving distinctions between findings that can occur together.

Our work in the **RSNA Knee Abnormality Detection competition** explored this problem through a notebook combining several publicly available pretrained models. The best public leaderboard score we recorded was **0.956**. It was not a leading competition entry, but it provided a practical foundation for investigating how image models can be integrated, evaluated, and challenged by new experiments.

This is a competition research result. It does not establish clinical effectiveness, regulatory readiness, or a final private leaderboard position.

# Twelve findings one examination

The challenge asks models to predict twelve clinically relevant knee findings. RSNA describes a dataset pairing MRI examinations with radiology reports, creating opportunities to learn from images and clinical language. The competition metric is the mean of twelve finding-specific ROC-AUC values. [RSNA challenge overview](https://www.rsna.org/artificial-intelligence/ai-image-challenge/knee-mri-ai-challenge), [Kaggle competition](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection/overview).


|  |  |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| **Category** | **Findings** |
| Ligaments | ACL and MCL abnormalities |
| Menisci | Medial and lateral meniscal abnormalities |
| Osteoarthritis | Medial, lateral, and patellofemoral compartments |
| Fluid and inflammation | Effusion and synovitis |
| Other findings | Baker’s cyst, contusion, and fracture |


 

This is **multi-label classification**: an examination can have several positive findings. The model produces a score for each target rather than choosing one mutually exclusive diagnosis.

That distinction changes evaluation. A system might recognize an effusion well while struggling with a ligament injury. Averaging performance across findings makes those differences matter, even when a finding is uncommon.

# What 0956 actually means

Our reported **0.956 is a public leaderboard macro ROC-AUC**, not 95.6% diagnostic accuracy.

For one finding, AUC measures how well scores rank positive examinations above negative ones across possible thresholds. The competition averages twelve such values. It does not specify a clinical operating threshold, the number of missed injuries, or the reliability of an individual patient’s score.

A clinical service would need additional measurements: sensitivity and specificity at a chosen threshold, predictive values in its patient population, calibration, and subgroup performance.

During our participation, the leaderboard notice stated that approximately 30% of test data determined the public score, with the remaining 70% reserved for final evaluation. We therefore report **the observed public result only**. A rounded score cannot establish that two models make identical predictions or generalize equally well.

# Inside the notebook a rank-based ensemble

The scored pipeline combined an **R7 ensemble**, **Raptor384**, and **Raptor224**. These were existing public model resources integrated into our notebook workflow. Our contribution was the surrounding ensemble configuration, execution, checks, and subsequent experimentation; we do not claim to have originated the underlying public architectures or pretrained weights.

![](/src/uploads/pipeline.svg)

*Figure 2. With complete model coverage, the nominal shares were 50% R7, 32.5% Raptor384, and 17.5% Raptor224. The later ConvNeXt experiment did not enter the retained submission.*

## Organize the MRI data and execute each branch

The notebook resolved competition studies, executed model-specific image readers and inference routines, and associated outputs with the correct study identifiers. MRI examinations contain multiple series; preprocessing requirements differ between model branches.

The two Raptor branches used different input resolutions. Combining them with R7 supplied several sets of predictions for the same targets. Different configurations can make different errors, but their usefulness together must be measured rather than assumed.

## Check identifiers, columns, and coverage

Prediction tables were reordered against the test-study list before blending. Checks covered study identifiers, finding columns, finite values, and score ranges. Coverage and failure information were recorded separately.

A correctly trained network can still produce an invalid submission if its output rows are joined incorrectly. These checks address that engineering risk; they do not establish diagnostic performance.

## Blend percentile ranks

Raw scores from different models need not share the same scale. One may produce many values near zero or one, while another produces a narrower range. The notebook converted predictions into within-finding percentile ranks before blending.

With all branches available, its nominal combination was:

**Final score = 0.50 × rank(R7) + 0.325 × rank(Raptor384) + 0.175 × rank(Raptor224).**

The Raptor allocation was split 65:35 between its 384 and 224 branches. These were fixed settings, not weights established by an independent optimization study. The implementation also tracked missing predictions and applied its declared failure-handling rules.

Rank blending is suited to an evaluation based on ordering, but its outputs should not be interpreted as calibrated disease probabilities. A combination is useful only when an appropriate evaluation supports it.

## Produce the submission

The notebook wrote submission.csv with one row per study and twelve finding scores. Logged coverage and output checks made inference easier to inspect and reproduce. The author-observed public leaderboard result for the retained ensemble was 0.956.

The original resources deserve explicit credit: [R7 model bundle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/heliosli/rsna-knee-compact-r7cnxfsss), [R7 supporting code](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/heliosli/rsna-orthofoundation-fold0-epoch7-20261004), and [Raptor weights](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/nartaa/rsna-knee-publication-swa-weights-20261007). Reuse and redistribution remain subject to their respective terms.

# What the next experiment taught us

We subsequently trained a separate ConvNeXt-Tiny branch using sagittal and coronal stacks: 24 input channels, three folds, and eight epochs per fold. Supervision came from the public [11-label evidence-fusion dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/omerzalman/rsna-knee-11-label-evidence-fusion). That source excluded synovitis, so the experiment did not train a new synovitis predictor.

The fit used 4,345 studies after excluding the 58 expert-panel studies and linked report groups. Auditing the supplied prediction tables found the expected identifiers, valid values, and no report groups crossing the declared folds. Those checks establish consistency of the tables, not independent clinical validity or proof of every training operation.

The new branch achieved approximately **0.804 macro AUC across eleven findings on the 58-study expert panel**. This is a different evaluation from the competition score and cannot be compared directly with 0.956.

The relevant within-panel comparison tested a fixed 5% contribution to the original ensemble:


|  |  |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| **Same expert-panel comparison, twelve findings** | **Macro AUC** |
| Original ensemble | 0.936479 |
| Ensemble with experimental contribution | 0.935209 |
| Difference | −0.001270 |


 

The paired bootstrap interval for the difference crossed zero. The experiment did not support adopting the contribution, so the notebook retained the baseline predictions.

This was a negative result. Training learned patterns in the pseudo-targets, but it did not deliver a demonstrated ensemble improvement. The small, repeatedly used panel and uncertain public-model training exposure also limit what these diagnostics establish. Adding another model is not, by itself, an innovation that improves performance.

# Where medical imaging AI could help

Knee MRI AI has an important research precedent. MRNet demonstrated retrospective deep-learning classification of knee abnormalities and investigated radiologist performance with model assistance. It supports studying AI as a reader aid; its results should not be transferred automatically to a different model or hospital. [Bien et al., PLOS Medicine, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1002699).

For appropriately developed and evaluated systems, several applications merit investigation:

·       **A structured second read.** Finding-specific scores could prompt a clinician to revisit a potentially overlooked structure.

·       **Worklist support.** A separately evaluated triage tool could help prioritize examinations if urgent findings are detected at an acceptable sensitivity.

·       **Research cohort discovery.** Image-derived labels could help researchers identify candidate studies for expert review.

·       **Learning from clinical language.** Reports can provide supervision at scale, although derived targets require auditing for omissions, ambiguity, and disagreement with image-based reference labels.

These are proposed uses, not benefits demonstrated by our notebook. Whether a tool helps depends on its task, the reader, its operating threshold, and the consequences of false positives and false negatives. The broader case for healthcare AI emphasizes combining computational capability with clinical judgment and evaluating its effects on care. [Topol, Nature Medicine, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-018-0300-7).

# From a competition notebook to a clinical study

A meaningful next step would be evaluation around a specific intended use. It would require an independent patient cohort, documented reference-label procedures, and testing across relevant scanners, acquisition protocols, institutions, and patient groups. Earlier research on chest radiograph models showed that performance can vary across hospital systems, illustrating why success on one dataset does not guarantee transfer. [Zech et al., PLOS Medicine, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1002683).

Before deployment, operating thresholds, calibration, and subgroup errors would need examination. A prospective workflow study should ask whether assistance improves decisions or efficiency without introducing unacceptable harms.

Reporting and deployment frameworks provide useful structure. **CLAIM 2024** addresses transparent reporting of medical imaging AI studies. **FUTURE-AI** extends attention across development and deployment, including fairness, robustness, traceability, usability, and monitoring. These frameworks help define the evidence still needed. [Tejani et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.1148/ryai.240300), [Lekadir et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2024-081554).

# What we take forward

Our 0.956 public leaderboard AUC is an empirical outcome for one ensemble and competition setting. The unsuccessful follow-up experiment is equally informative: adding a model, training longer, or reducing training loss does not guarantee better classification on the population that matters.

For TerminalBio, the practical lesson is to connect model development with clear evaluation questions. Medical image recognition becomes useful when it reliably supports a defined decision, under conditions resembling real care, with its limitations visible to the people using it.
